questions.question: In a bookings_flat table that stores room_type alongside every booking row, what normalization violation exists, and what's the risk?
options: 1NF violation -- room_type holds multiple values
3NF violation -- room_type depends on room_number (a non-key column), not directly on booking_id, so updating a room's type requires updating every booking row for that room or risking inconsistency
No violation -- this is a normal denormalized reporting table
2NF violation because booking_id is a composite key
questions.explanation: room_type is transitively dependent on room_number rather than the booking's own key. The fix is moving room_type into a separate rooms table referenced by foreign key, so it's stored exactly once per room.

questions.question: Why is the btree_gist extension required before creating EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)?
options: It speeds up the query planner for unrelated joins
GiST indexes natively support range types but need btree_gist to also index ordinary scalar types like the integer room_id, so the equality and overlap checks can be combined in one index
It is required to use the TSTZRANGE data type at all
It enables row-level security on the bookings table
questions.explanation: Without btree_gist, Postgres raises 'data type integer has no default operator class for access method gist' because GiST doesn't know how to index a plain integer for equality comparison until the extension supplies that operator class.

questions.question: A booking is stored as '[2024-01-01 10:00, 2024-01-01 12:00)' and another booking for the same room is '[2024-01-01 12:00, 2024-01-01 14:00)'. Does the exclusion constraint reject the second insert?
options: Yes, because both ranges contain 12:00
No, because the half-open [) convention excludes 12:00 from the first range, so the two ranges share no overlapping instant
Yes, but only if the rows are inserted in the same transaction
It depends on the server's timezone setting
questions.explanation: Half-open ranges include the lower bound and exclude the upper bound. This lets back-to-back bookings share a boundary timestamp without being treated as overlapping -- exactly the behavior a scheduling system needs.

questions.question: In the audit trigger example, why does the trigger use a WHEN (OLD.balance IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.balance) clause?
options: To make the trigger run faster on large tables
To prevent the trigger body from inserting an audit row when an UPDATE touches the accounts table but doesn't actually change the balance value
Because triggers cannot reference OLD and NEW without a WHEN clause
To convert the trigger into a STATEMENT-level trigger
questions.explanation: Without the WHEN guard, any UPDATE to accounts -- even one only changing the owner name -- would fire the trigger and write a spurious audit row claiming the balance changed (with old_balance equal to new_balance). The WHEN clause scopes the trigger to only the relevant case.

questions.question: A sales table is PARTITION BY LIST (region) with explicit partitions for 'US' and 'EU' only, and no DEFAULT partition. What happens when you INSERT a row with region = 'APAC'?
options: It is silently dropped
It is automatically routed to a new partition created on the fly
The INSERT fails with an error like 'no partition of relation "sales" found for row'
It is stored in the US partition as a fallback
questions.explanation: Without a DEFAULT partition, any row whose partition key doesn't match an existing bound has nowhere to go and the INSERT fails outright. Creating a DEFAULT partition during initial design is the standard safety net against this.

questions.question: Per the decision table in this lesson, which mechanism is recommended for 'no two rows with overlapping time ranges per room' specifically because constraints vs triggers differ in concurrency safety?
options: An application-level check before INSERT
An EXCLUDE constraint, because it is enforced atomically by the database engine itself, closing the race condition that two concurrent transactions checking-then-inserting would otherwise hit
A STATEMENT-level AFTER trigger
A CHECK constraint with a subquery
questions.explanation: Application-level 'check then insert' logic has a race condition: two concurrent requests can both pass the check before either writes. An EXCLUDE constraint pushes the conflict detection into the atomic INSERT operation itself, where no race window exists.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn that EXCLUDE constraints have a portability caveat across SQL dialects?
options: EXCLUDE constraints are deprecated in newer Postgres versions

EXCLUDE constraints are a PostgreSQL-specific feature relying on GiST indexes and range types; migrating the same overlap-prevention logic to MySQL or SQL Server requires a different implementation (e.g., triggers or computed-column unique indexes)
EXCLUDE constraints only work with integer columns
EXCLUDE constraints require a paid Postgres license
questions.explanation: EXCLUDE is not part of the ANSI SQL standard. Some managed cloud Postgres offerings also restrict the btree_gist extension needed alongside it, so teams should verify extension availability before designing around this pattern.

questions.question: What privilege risk does a trigger function marked SECURITY DEFINER introduce?
options: It runs slower than a normal function

It executes with the privileges of the function's owner rather than the caller, so a bug or injected input in that function runs with elevated access -- search_path should be set explicitly to prevent schema-spoofing
It cannot access the OLD or NEW row variables
It automatically grants the caller superuser access
questions.explanation: SECURITY DEFINER is sometimes necessary (e.g., letting a low-privilege role write to a restricted audit table), but it means the function's code runs with elevated rights regardless of who calls it -- a real privilege-escalation risk if the function isn't carefully written and search_path-pinned.
